speaker: Paul H. Sinclair
title: Quick to Help, Slow to Judge
summary: Elder Sinclair teaches that a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge. He tells of a Primary boy who buttoned his sleeve to his lapel, and of the little girl who freed him while Elder Sinclair only felt annoyed; then he shows the Savior offering the woman at the well living water instead of judgment. He asks members to help friends and new members the same way, so the people at today's wells feel they have come home.

findings.quote: President Dallin H. Oaks taught the following about being slow to judge others: “We must refrain from making final judgments on people because we lack the knowledge and the wisdom to do so. … The Lord’s way of final judgment will be to apply His perfect knowledge of the law a person has received and to judge on the basis of that person’s circumstances, motives, and actions throughout his or her entire life” (“‘Judge Not’ and Judging,” Ensign, Aug. 1999, 8; see also Matthew 7:1–5; Luke 6:37–42; 3 Nephi 14:1–12; Mormon 8:20). Likewise, Jesus consistently taught that helping others should be a hallmark of our discipleship (see Matthew 5:38–47; Mark 10:45; Luke 10:30–37). In the Book of Mormon, this characteristic of discipleship is taught in many passages, including the beautiful descriptions of the ways we can live the covenant we make at baptism. These passages illustrate many ways in which we help and serve others (see Mosiah 18:8–11; see also Jacob 2:17–19; Alma 1:26–27; 3 Nephi 13:1–4). Jesus Christ showed us the perfect example of helping without judging when He appeared to the Nephites and “tarr[ied] a little longer with them” (3 Nephi 17:5). Sparing any judgment, He ministered to every need and healed each wound simply because He was “filled with compassion” and “mercy” (3 Nephi 17:6, 7).
findings.note: Quotes President Oaks on refraining from final judgments

findings.quote: By the time the Savior met the woman at the well, the cultural and religious animosity between Jews and Samaritans was entrenched. As President Dallin H. Oaks summarized it, Samaritans “belonged to a group the Jews isolated and held in contempt” (“Alive in Christ,” Liahona, May 2026, 85). Thus, it was revealing that Jesus determined that He “had to go through Samaria” (John 4:4, New International Version; emphasis added). His decision to go intentionally to Samaria and speak to a Samaritan woman was socially radical and spiritually profound. President Oaks further taught in the April 2026 general conference that being alive in Christ includes being peacemakers (see “Alive in Christ,” 85–87). How remarkable, yet completely unsurprising, that one of the early acts of the Savior’s earthly ministry was to be a peacemaker with the woman at the well.
findings.note: Quotes President Oaks on Jews and Samaritans, and on being peacemakers

findings.quote: There is an idiom in English and in many European languages that one should not “go to the well one too many times.” The idiom attempts to teach the principle that a person who goes too frequently to the same source of help risks depleting the value of the source until it ultimately fails (see The Free Dictionary, “go to the well too many times,” idioms.thefreedictionary.com). While the idiom is useful for describing worldly resources, it does not apply when speaking of Jesus Christ. We can never go to our own well to meet Him too many times (see Mosiah 26:30). Our effort to access Jesus Christ’s Atonement does not deplete its effectiveness, because it is infinite. Describing the glorious connection between the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the nonjudgmental help received by his brother who was dying of cancer, Bishop W. Christopher Waddell said: “Thanks to wonderful men and women who saw a need, did not judge, and ministered like the Savior, it wasn’t too late for Mike. … We must remember that it is never too late and no one has ever wandered so far from the path that he or she is beyond the reach of the infinite Atonement of Jesus Christ, which is limitless in its duration and scope” (“Just as He Did,” Liahona, May 2019, 21; emphasis added).
findings.note: The well idiom, then Bishop Waddell on his brother Mike and the limitless Atonement

findings.quote: As part of His offer of help, the Savior was unafraid to invite this new disciple to accept a responsibility (see John 4:7). Though the woman did not immediately respond positively to Jesus’s request, over time and with one-on-one nurturing, the woman eventually, and joyfully, accepted the most significant of assignments: to tell the world that Jesus is the Messiah. As true followers of Jesus Christ and His example, we should be unafraid to invite people, especially new members, to serve and help others as part of their journey on the covenant path (see Mosiah 5:2; see also Dale G. Renlund, “Preserving the Heart’s Mighty Change,” Liahona, Nov. 2009, 99).
Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ recognize our potential to grow into the best possible version of ourselves (see Dale G. Renlund, “Personal Preparation to Meet the Savior,” Liahona, May 2025, 44).
findings.ref: Personal Preparation to Meet the Savior

findings.quote: Unsurprisingly, as He interacts with the woman at the well, the Savior exemplifies what has become known as “the missionary purpose.” Chapter 1 of Preach My Gospel teaches that the missionary purpose is to “invite others to come unto Christ by helping them receive the restored gospel through faith in Jesus Christ and His Atonement, repentance, baptism, receiving the gift of the Holy Ghost, and enduring to the end” (Preach My Gospel: A Guide to Sharing the Gospel of Jesus Christ [2023], 1; emphasis added). Jesus invites the woman at the well to come unto Him and then helps her to do so.
findings.ref: Preach My Gospel: A Guide to Sharing the Gospel of Jesus Christ

findings.quote: Elder Quentin L. Cook reported that over a period of three years, nearly 900,000 people came into covenant as converts to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (see “The Lord Is Hastening His Work,” Liahona, Nov. 2025, 48). At some point, each of those new members was, in his or her own way, a man or woman at the well.
findings.ref: The Lord Is Hastening His Work

findings.quote: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf summarized how our small, sometimes unnoticed gifts allow us to do simple things that represent the kind of help needed to change lives: “May I share with you some spiritual gifts that I have noticed in so many members across the world? Contemplate whether you have been blessed with one or more gifts like: Showing compassion. Noticing people who are overlooked. … Giving sincere compliments. … Explaining things simply. … Helping others know that they belong. … I hope you can see how precious [these gifts] are to the Lord’s work and how you might have touched, blessed, or even saved one of God’s children by your gifts” (“Do Your Part with All Your Heart,” Liahona, Nov. 2025, 23; see also Gerrit W. Gong, “No One Sits Alone,” Liahona, Nov. 2025, 40–43). In section 46 of the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord emphasizes that the real purpose for our spiritual gifts, be they large or small, is to help Heavenly Father’s children (see Doctrine and Covenants 46:8–10, 26).
findings.ref: Do Your Part with All Your Heart

findings.quote: President D. Todd Christofferson taught: “Adopting the character of Christ is not only a question of our personal preparation but a primary element of preparing the world for the Lord’s return and His glorious millennial reign. We tend to underestimate the influence of Christlike individuals in the world, but working one by one has always been Jesus’s approach to changing society and establishing His kingdom” (“The Character of Christ,” Liahona, May 2026, 91).
